title: Wealth stays behind
hookLine: riches, youth and power are left behind (Sukhmani 19)

lines: GIVE IT BACK IN THE NEXT WORLD.
cards: Sikhs tell a story about a rich man in Lahore named Duni Chand. He was so wealthy that he flew flags over his house, one for every large sum he owned.
When Guru Nanak came through the city, Duni Chand invited him to a grand meal and asked if there was anything he could do for him. Guru Nanak handed him a small sewing needle.
Keep this for me, he said, and give it back to me in the next world. Duni Chand happily agreed. Then he went home, looked at the needle, and couldn't sleep.

teach.h: HOW WILL YOU CARRY A NEEDLE?
teach.b: In the story, Duni Chand's wife asks what's wrong, and he shows her the needle. She asks the obvious question: how exactly are you going to carry a needle into the next world? He goes back to Guru Nanak.
I can't take this with me. And Guru Nanak answers: if you can't take a needle, how will you take all those flags?

teach.h: A PICTURE, NOT A COURT RECORD.
teach.b: It's a janamsakhi story, from the old tellings of Guru Nanak's life, and like many of them it's a picture, not a court record. But it says in one small object what the nineteenth ashtpadi says in its stanzas.
Riches stay behind. So do youth, beauty and power. Gurbani comes back to it: the body we're proud of, the house we built, the position we fought for, none of it comes along.
And notice the needle. It's about as small and light as a thing can be. If even that stays, everything stays.
The story is gentle with Duni Chand. Nobody shames him. The tradition says he took the lesson and began giving his wealth to feed people.
Sikhs draw a practical turn from it. If wealth stays behind anyway, the question becomes what you do with it while you hold it.
Sikh tradition encourages dasvandh, giving a tenth of what you earn, and the langar exists because people give. Giving something away isn't losing it.
It was always going to be left behind. Giving just chooses where it lands.

how: Sikhs tell the janamsakhi story of Duni Chand and the needle, and many practice dasvandh, giving a tenth of their earnings; Sukhmani's nineteenth ashtpadi names riches, youth and power as things left behind.

o: giving a tenth of what you earn
an inheritance split among ten heirs
a tax paid to the ruler of Lahore

games.q: wealth stays behind — tap the pairs.
p: give it back in the next world

s: in the story, Guru Nanak shames Duni Chand in public
the story is gentle; tradition says he began giving his wealth to feed people.
the Duni Chand story comes from the janamsakhis
the old tellings of Guru Nanak's life.
the nineteenth ashtpadi says youth and power come with us
riches, youth and power are all left behind.

games.q: you're Duni Chand, holding the needle at midnight. what do you realize?
o: I'll find a way to carry it.
if I can't take a needle, I can't take any of it.
games.why: if even the smallest needle stays, everything stays. the story says Duni Chand began giving his wealth away.

practice: Let one of the things you own rise up, a coat you don't wear, a book you've finished, a tool someone else could use, some money you could spare; not the hardest thing, just one real thing.
Picture it in someone else's hands, being used, and notice how that feels.

wordCard.voice: Dasvandh, the practice of giving a tenth of what you earn: since riches, youth and power all stay behind, even a needle, the question is where you let your wealth land.

orig.note: Punjabi: dasvandh, a tenth part, the Sikh practice of giving a tenth of one's earnings.

carryVoice: Your line: left behind. If a needle can't go along, neither can the flags. Day five hundred eleven.
